paper_title: EvoWeb: A Benchmark for Coding Agents on Evolving Web Applications

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Web application development often proceeds through successive requests that extend an existing implementation. Yet web-generation benchmarks primarily evaluate development toward fixed specifications. We introduce EvoWeb, a novel benchmark comprising 320 cumulative requests over 32 web applications, grounded in real-world product features and structured by functional dependency graphs. Agents iteratively modify a persistent codebase, while a multimodal web agent tests each intermediate application in a live browser, assessing newly requested functionality, cross-request integration, and previously requested functionality. To characterize reliability throughout development, we integrate trajectory performance across user-tolerance thresholds rather than impose a fixed stopping criterion. Experiments across open- and closed-source frontier models show that EvoWeb reveals clear performance differences between models, with cross-request integration emerging as a key challenge. Further analysis shows that later requests with deeper or more numerous dependencies are solved less accurately, while runtime errors become more frequent over successive requests. EvoWeb provides a testbed for evaluating and improving coding agents in long-horizon, multi-request development.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models are increasingly used as agents for end-to-end software development, where they are responsible not only for generating code but for translating high-level user requests into complete, working applications. Systems such as Bolt.new and Lovable make this capability accessible to users with limited or no programming expertise through natural-language interaction. Users describe the functionality and appearance they want, while the agent decides how to implement them and is responsible for producing working application (Lu et al., 2026b). Development in this setting often continues beyond the initial request. Users return to add features, modify existing behavior, and extend functionality introduced earlier. This changes what it means to evaluate coding agent. later request may depend on state, interfaces, or behavior that the same agent implemented several requests earlier. new feature may work on its own but fail when it needs to use that earlier functionality. It may also break behavior that previously worked. Evaluating requests independently therefore does not capture whether an agent can continue extending its own application while making functionality introduced at different points work together. Existing web-generation benchmarks evaluate either applications produced from single high-level request (Lu et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026; Tran et al., 2026) or multiple interactions that refine an application toward an existing specification or user intent (Lu et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026). Persistent multi-request development has also been studied in software engineering (Shen et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Sobal et al., 2026; Orlanski et al., 2026). None of these targets user-facing web applications that evolve through successive requests. This leaves central question: How reliably can coding agents extend persistent application over successive user requests while integrating with previously implemented functionality and preserving existing behavior? We introduce EVOWEB, benchmark for evaluating coding agents on evolving web applications. EVOWEB contains 320 cumulative requests over 32 applications. Starting from an initial application specification, we ground follow-up requests in functionality observed in real-world web appli-

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: EVOWEB pipeline. (A) Construction: for each seed prompt, features from two similar real websites are used to plan dependency DAG and write ten requests, which are automatically verified, repaired, and human-curated. (B) Evaluation: coding agent solves them one at time, browser agent runs five tests after each, and scores are averaged over user-tolerance thresholds. cations, so that applications grow through plausible product features. We jointly construct each request sequence, its verification tests, and directed acyclic graph (DAG) of functional dependencies, where an edge indicates that later request requires functionality introduced by an earlier one. The resulting sequences undergo automated verification and repair followed by human curation. The DAG is hidden from the agent, which receives requests sequentially and modifies the application produced by all preceding requests. For each follow-up request, we define five browser-based verification tests: three test the newly requested functionality, one exercises its integration with earlier functionality along dependency in the DAG, and one re-tests functionality requested earlier. After every request, these tests are executed against the resulting application in the browser. This allows us to distinguish whether the agent can implement new functionality, deliver earlier-requested functionality in the current application, and correctly compose functionality introduced across different points in the development trajectory. Sequential evaluation also requires deciding what happens after an intermediate failure. Stopping at the first failure assumes that the user abandons development immediately, while continuing regardless of quality assumes that the user always continues. More generally, the measured trajectory can depend on the success threshold used to decide whether development continues. We therefore evaluate each trajectory across range of user-tolerance thresholds and integrate performance over these thresholds. This avoids committing to single stopping rule. Our evaluation of 14 coding models on EVOWEB shows that reliably extending an application across successive requests remains challenging. Fable 5 and Kimi K3 lead with Grades of 0.694 and 0.684. Cross-request integration consistently scores lower than new or earlier-requested functionality, highlighting the difficulty of making features introduced at different stages work together. Among later requests, accuracy also declines with dependency depth and the number of earlier requests they depend on. Additionally, we observe runtime errors become more frequent over successive requests, while build failures remain rare for most models. These performance differences are not simply matter of generation effort: Fable 5 scores at the top while using the fewest agent turns and less than half the output tokens of Sonnet 4.6. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: Benchmark. We introduce EVOWEB, benchmark of 320 cumulative requests over 32 web applications, for evaluating coding agents as applications evolve. Methodology. We develop methodology for constructing and evaluating multi-request development trajectories, including DAG-structured dependencies across requests and tolerance-averaged metrics that capture trajectory performance. Empirical study. We provide broad empirical study of coding agents on evolving web applications and find that cross-request integration is consistently harder than implementing new functionality

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Coding agents and long-horizon software engineering. Evaluation of coding models has progressed from isolated code generation to agentic software engineering, where models modify repositories, execute programs, and iteratively refine their solutions. SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) evaluates repository-level issue resolution, while more recent benchmarks extend the horizon of the work itself: SWE-EVO (Le et al., 2025) specifies an entire software release, and SWE-Marathon (Desai et al., 2026) studies ultra-long-horizon software tasks. Other work explicitly evaluates sequences of interactions over persistent state. EvoCode-Bench (Shen et al., 2026) maintains one workspace and agent session across 515 requests, SWE-Together (Wu et al., 2026) reconstructs multi-request development sequences from recorded useragent interactions, and StaminaBench (Sobal et al., 2026) and SlopCodeBench (Orlanski et al., 2026) study degradation over increasingly long interaction horizons. These works establish the importance of evaluating coding agents beyond individual tasks. EVOWEB studies this problem in web development, where agents must repeatedly extend the application they themselves have built. Web-application generation and evolving requirements. Web-generation benchmarks evaluate complete applications through observable behavior. WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2026b) pairs websitegeneration requests with GUI tests executed against live applications, with subsequent work providing finer-grained functional evaluation (Liu et al., 2026; Tran et al., 2026). Web-Bench (Xu et al., 2025) also considers sequentially dependent web-development tasks, but its tasks are formulated primarily as developer-facing specifications that often prescribe implementation details (example in App. A). In contrast, EVOWEB requests are written at the user level: they fix the expected behavior, including seed data where tests need exact values, but never prescribe the implementation (files, components, class names, or layout), and their features are grounded in real-world websites. Other benchmarks introduce iteration primarily as refinement toward an existing intent: WebGen-Agent (Lu et al., 2026a) repeatedly improves an application against fixed request; AsukaBench (Wang et al., 2026) progressively exposes predefined product specification through feedback; and ICAE-Bench (Peng et al., 2026) reveals requirements drawn from an existing repository. In EVOWEB, each request may introduce new functionality and is applied to the codebase produced by all preceding requests. Dependencies among requests are represented as DAG, where an edge indicates that functionality requested at relies on functionality introduced at i. Unlike DAGs used to organize evaluation criteria, such as in Asuka-Bench (Wang et al., 2026), our DAG captures dependencies in the applications evolution, is hidden from the evaluated agent, and supports tests that directly exercise cross-request integration. Thus, each model must continually extend its accumulated implementation while integrating new functionality with what it built earlier. Evaluating sequential development and user tolerance. Sequential benchmarks must decide what happens after an intermediate failure. Web-Bench (Xu et al., 2025) and EvoCode-Bench (Shen et al., 2026), for example, terminate trajectory after failed verifier, while independently scoring

These correspond to extreme user models: one abandons the application when request falls below fixed pass criterion, while the other tolerates any failure. EVOWEB instead scores each request from browser-observed behavior on graded scale, allowing the stopping rule itself to vary. For tolerance threshold t, the user continues while request quality remains above and leaves otherwise. Because the tolerance of the user population is unknown, we run all requests ungated, replay all thresholds offline, and integrate performance over t. Threshold integration also appears in selective prediction (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017; Traub et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025) and budget-constrained agent evaluation via the area under performance-versus-budget curves (Cai et al., 2025), while multi-turn safety evaluation tracks survival over turns at fixed failure threshold (Hu et al., 2026). These works sweep property of the system, such as an abstention threshold or compute budget, or fix the threshold, whereas we sweep property of the user: the minimum quality they accept before abandoning the application. Our Grade and Survival scores therefore summarize long-horizon performance across user tolerances without committing to an arbitrary stopping rule. Table 1 summarizes the comparison.

sections.title: 3 EVOWEB BENCHMARK
sections.content: We design EVOWEB around three desiderata that we argue are essential for evaluating contemporary web-development agents. Realistic: applications are grounded in real-world use cases, while follow-up requests are derived from functionality observed in real products, reflecting how users iteratively develop web applications through high-level natural-language requests. Cumulative: requests form long-horizon, interdependent sequences in which each new feature must be integrated with an evolving application while preserving previously implemented functionality. This setting tests whether agents can maintain correctness and coherence as the codebase grows, rather than solving each request in isolation. Agentic: each request is addressed through contemporary coding-agent scaffold rather than single model invocation, allowing the model to interact with the repository, execution environment, and other available tools over multiple steps, as is characteristic of modern coding-agent deployments. In what follows, we describe data curation (Sec. 3.1), the harness (Sec. 3.2), the functional judge (Sec. 3.3), and our metrics (Sec. 3.4).

sections.title: 3.1 DATA CURATION
sections.content: Grounding in real web-apps. We randomly subsample 40 of the 101 initial application specifications in WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2026b). Following automated verification and repair, followed by human curation, we retain 32 application trajectories (320 requests) spanning 16 of its 20 domains. We treat each selected specification as seed: an initial application description that we extend into sequence of ten requests. To ensure that these requests correspond to capabilities found in real applications, we ground their design in deployed web-apps. For each seed application, retrieval agent (Sonnet 4.6 with web search and page fetching tools) identifies two existing websites with similar purpose and extracts three to four notable features from each that extend beyond the seed specification. generator model (Fable 5) then adapts these features into follow-up requests for the benchmark. This grounding makes the resulting requests more representative of how real products evolve and, importantly, prevents different applications from collapsing to the same small set of generic additions. We describe the application selection and domain distribution in App. B, the retrieval procedure in App. C, and study the effect of grounding in App. C.1.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Dependencies between requests. Grounding determines which features should be added to each application; we next determine how those features should depend on one another as the application evolves. In real applications, later functionality often relies on state, interfaces, or behavior introduced earlier. We therefore explicitly structure each request sequence as directed acyclic graph (DAG) of feature dependencies. Before generating the natural-language requests, the generator constructs DAG whose nodes correspond to the ten requested features and whose edges encode functional dependencies: an edge indicates that request cannot be implemented correctly without functionality introduced by request i. We require these dependencies to be substantive rather than superficial; for example, merely operating on the same underlying data does not constitute an edge. To ensure that each sequence contains meaningful long-range dependencies, we require the DAG to contain dependency chain of depth at least three and at least three later requests that depend on functionality introduced earlier. We validate the resulting DAG with separate LLM-based verifier that is given the proposed feature dependencies and the constraints above. Sequences that fail verification undergo one automated revision and are discarded if they remain invalid. Human curators subsequently review all retained sequences and finalize their dependency structure and verification tests. The DAG is used only during benchmark construction and analysis and is never exposed to the evaluated agent. This design allows EVOWEB to test whether agents can extend an evolving application while correctly reusing and preserving functionality introduced in earlier requests. We study these dependencies in Sec. 5.1; App. specifies the generation and verification procedure. Verification of incremental functionality. The sequential and dependent structure of EVOWEB also changes how each request must be evaluated. We build on the functional evaluation protocol of WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2026b), which represents each test case as UI operation paired with an expected outcome and uses WebVoyager (He et al., 2024) to execute the test. WebGen-Bench constructs such tests to cover the requirements of single, from-scratch application specification; our setting instead requires evaluating feature added to an already evolving application. We therefore design five verification tests for each follow-up request: three test the newly introduced functionality, one tests its integration with an earlier feature along dependency in the DAG, and one backward test re-runs test from an earlier request. Because it scores earlier functionality in the current application, failure may reflect either regression or functionality that was never implemented, and pass may follow later repair; with one such test per request, it samples earlier functionality rather than exhaustively auditing regressions (verdict transitions in App. D.1). For the 6% of requests with no incoming dependency, the integration test instead checks global rule introduced earlier (App. D). To isolate the behavior under evaluation, we place any prerequisite application state directly in the user request as seed data, rather than asking the evaluator to construct it through the UI. This keeps each test focused on the requested functionality and avoids conflating failures in test setup with failures of the feature itself. All tests are designed to be short and implementation-agnostic. Together, these design choices yield benchmark of grounded, interdependent request sequences with verification tailored to incremental development. Figure 1 summarizes the construction pipeline, while Table 8 reports the resulting dataset composition and dependency statistics.

sections.title: 3.2 AGENTIC HARNESS
sections.content: Prior web-generation benchmarks primarily evaluate applications generated from single user request. In WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2026b), its best-performing Bolt.diy configuration follows two-stage generation procedure: the model first selects starter template and then generates the application from it. In EVOWEB, each request is instead implemented through multi-turn agentic interaction. The model can repeatedly inspect and modify the repository, execute commands, observe their outputs, and revise its implementation before completing the request. The repository and the conversation history persist across requests, so each interaction operates on the application produced by all preceding requests (execution details in App. E). The agent receives no feedback on test outcomes between requests, so each request also measures how well it maintains what it has already built. Importantly, the first request in every flow is the original WebGen-Bench instruction, allowing us to directly examine the effect of the interaction protocol before any cross-request dependencies arise. On the shared initial requests, Haiku 4.5 achieves substantially higher functional accuracy with our multi-turn agentic harness than with the WebGen-Bench configuration. This observation motivates our use of an interaction protocol that allows models to inspect, execute, and iteratively refine their implementations.

sections.title: 3.3 REQUEST EVALUATION
sections.content: After each request, we evaluate whether the resulting application satisfies it. We follow the evaluation protocol of WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2026b): WebVoyager agent (He et al., 2024) observes the interface through Set-of-Marks representation, executes each test in the browser through Selenium, and returns YES, PARTIAL, or NO depending on whether the expected outcome is observed. We run it with stronger computer-use backbone, Sonnet 4.6, which is among the strongest models on OSWorld-Verified (on par with Opus 4.6; Xie et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2026) at lower cost. WebGen-Bench validated this protocol against human annotators, reporting 8694% agreement, and we report blinded human audit of the evaluator on EVOWEB in App. D.3.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Experimental setup. We evaluate 14 contemporary models on the 320 requests of EVOWEB. Each model is deployed with the OpenHands scaffold and is given budget of at most 20 agent turns for each request. The repository state is preserved across the ten requests in trajectory, such that every request is implemented on top of the application produced by the preceding interactions. After each request, we evaluate the resulting application in the browser using WebVoyager with Sonnet 4.6 as the underlying judge, following the verification protocol in Sec. 3.3 and Sec. 3.4. We keep the benchmark instances, scaffold, interaction budget, and functional evaluator fixed across models.

sections.title: 4.1 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: Overall performance. On Grade, our primary metric, Fable 5 (0.694) and Kimi K3 (0.684) lead, followed by GPT 5.6 Sol (0.622), while the weakest reaches only 0.162. We do not rank the top two, whose 0.010 gap is within run-to-run variation (App. F). Survival follows nearly the same order, with the best surviving about 7.3 of 10 requests (Table 2; standard deviations in App. F). Although every test is fully passed in some run (App. D), even the best models do not sustain high-quality functionality across the trajectory. Robustness to user tolerance. Figure 3 (left) sweeps the tolerance threshold for the closedsource models. Fable 5 leads at every t; GPT 5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6 stay close together throughout; and Haiku 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Luna remain well below. The gap between stronger and weaker models thus persists across the full tolerance range, although their exact ordering can change. App. reports mean accuracy (t = 0) and fail-stop scores (t = 1) for all models. Generation effort. Two of the three strongest models, Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, each produce only about 100K output tokens per trajectory, and Fable 5 also uses the fewest turns per request (4.7).

LLM judges are known to favor their own outputs (Zheng et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2024; Wataoka et al., 2024), which could bias EVOWEB toward the graders model family. We therefore re-evaluate all runs, replacing the Sonnet 4.6 judge of Sec. 4 with three judges from other vendors (App. I). Absolute scores shift with the judge, but each alternative judge flips only 2-3 of the 28 model pairs, all among GPT 5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6, which are within 0.015 Grade of each other. No judge favors its own family: Sonnet 4.6 ranks lower under its own judge than under two of the others. The ranking is thus not an artifact of the judges identity.

sections.title: 5.1 DAG-STRUCTURED REQUESTS ANALYSIS
sections.content: Later features often consume the state, behavior, or interfaces of earlier ones, so the agent must compose new functionality with what it has already built. We ask whether this composition is harder than implementing new feature or delivering earlier ones by comparing the three test types of Sec. 3.1: functional, backward, and integration, the last of which traverses DAG edge. We exclude the integration tests of requests with no incoming dependency (6%), which check global rule instead. For each type, we recompute Grade from that types outcomes alone while keeping each requests gate score gr(t) based on its full accuracy ar, so all three are compared over the same trajectories. Table 4 shows the same order for every model: backward tests score highest, followed by functional and then integration tests, with average Grade falling from 0.58 to 0.55 and 0.51. Dependencies thus add composition challenge beyond new or earlier functionality in isolation. Since integration tests are the hardest, we next ask whether accuracy drops with dependency. We use two properties of each requests DAG node: its depth, the longest dependency chain leading to it, and its in-degree, the number of earlier requests it directly relies on. To separate dependency from position in the trajectory, we use only the last requests (810), which also cover the widest range of both. Figure 4 plots their accuracy ar against each property, with linear fit per model. Every line slopes downward. Together with Table 4, this shows that difficulty compounds along the DAG: requests that build on more earlier functionality are harder, especially for weaker models.

sections.title: 5.2 BUILD AND RUNTIME ERRORS
sections.content: Functional tests show whether feature works, not whether failure comes from broken application. We therefore also record, after each request, whether the production build fails (build error) or the served application raises an uncaught exception, triggers React error boundary, or fails to load local module during browser evaluation (runtime error). An error counts only for the requests after which it is present (e.g., build error introduced at request 2 and fixed at request 3 counts for request 2 only); Table 2 reports the percentage of the 320 request instances with each error type. Build errors are rare for most models, whereas runtime errors vary far more and track Grade more closely (Spearman ρ = 0.72 vs. 0.52 for build errors). Qwen3.5 35B-A3B, for example, has build-error rate of 2.5% but runtime-error rate of 36.6%: models more often preserve buildable codebase than reliably executable one. Runtime errors also become more frequent as the application evolves, as the inset at right shows (runtime error rate by request index). By contrast, tool-call errors, i.e., failed tool executions such as string replacement that matches nothing, do not correlate with Grade (Spearman ρ = 0.06). The agent sees the failed call and repairs it in the next step, so these errors cost steps rather than quality.

sections.title: 5.3 FAILURE MODES IN EVOLVING APPLICATIONS
sections.content: To understand why tests fail, we use Sonnet 5 to classify the failed tests (score 0) of Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5 into app-side failure modes  (Table 5)  . Missing data/UI: record, field, page, or control the test needs does not exist. Incorrect data: the data exists, but value or computed result is wrong. Styling: color, font, layout, or label differs from the request. Runtime/build error: the app or route fails to build or crashes. State sync: an action is accepted, but the state or other views do not update. Unresponsive control: rendered control does not react to input. Haiku 4.5s failures are led by missing data (31.2%, vs. 21.323.6% for the other models), showing that the weakest model struggles to integrate features across requests: often, each page keeps its own copy of the data, so data added by one request never reaches pages added later. Fable 5, in contrast, rarely breaks the application (2.2% runtime or build errors, vs. 13.717.3% for the other models), and its failures shift toward incorrect values and styling, where it has the highest shares of all four models. It thus makes the application work but still fails on small details.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied how reliably coding agents can extend persistent web applications over successive requests while integrating new functionality and preserving earlier behavior. EVOWEB addresses this question through 320 cumulative requests across 32 applications grounded in real-world features and structured by functional dependencies. Browser-based tests assess each intermediate application, while tolerance-averaged metrics characterize trajectory performance without imposing single stopping threshold. Our experiments identify cross-request integration as consistent challenge: agents perform worse on composing features across requests than on new or earlier-requested functionality alone. Later requests with deeper or more numerous dependencies are also solved less accurately, and runtime errors become more frequent as requests accumulate despite generally low build-error rates. These findings highlight feature integration and sustained runtime reliability as priorities for improving coding agents. Looking ahead, extending EVOWEB to longer trajectories and closed-loop interaction, where users report failures and request repairs, would allow future work to examine whether agents can recover from mistakes while continuing to evolve an application.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: EVOWEB does not involve human subjects. The benchmark builds on public WebGen-Bench specifications and on publicly visible features of existing websites, and all seeded data are fictional, so it contains no personal information. The generated applications run locally without external services. We describe our use of large language models below.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: The construction of EVOWEB is described in Sec. 3.1, with the grounding procedure in App. and the full generation and verification specification in App. D; the complete generator, verifier, and grounding prompts are included in the supplementary material. The agentic harness, the evaluation protocol, and the metrics are specified in Sec. 3.23.4, and the experimental setup in Sec. 4. We report run-to-run variability in App. F, human validation of the evaluator in App. D.3, robustness to the judge model in App. I, and compute requirements in App. J. The dataset, including all requests, verification tests, dependency graphs, and pinned seeds, as well as the code for running and scoring agents, are available at the links on the first page.

sections.title: B APPLICATION SELECTION AND DOMAIN COVERAGE
sections.content: WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2026b) provides 101 application specifications across 20 domain classes, ranging from brochure sites and storefronts to dashboards, forums, and browser games. We randomly subsample 40 specifications and use each as seed for constructing candidate trajectory of ten cumulative user requests, following the procedure in Sec. 3.1. Verification and exclusions. Each candidate undergoes automated verification of its requests, dependency graph, and verification tests against the construction requirements. Candidates with identified violations receive one repair pass and are verified again. candidate is discarded if unresolved violations remain, such as dependencies on functionality not introduced by earlier requests, inconsistencies between seeded data and expected test outcomes, or tests that require behavior not specified in the requests. Human curators subsequently review the remaining candidates for coherence and suitability, excluding sequences whose follow-ups substantially duplicate existing functionality or whose dependencies remain contrived rather than reflecting plausible application development. Across these stages, eight candidate trajectories are excluded, leaving 32 in the final benchmark. Domain coverage. Figure 5 compares the domain distribution of the 32 retained trajectories with that of the full WebGen-Bench collection. The final benchmark covers 16 of the 20 domain classes. Under WebGen-Benchs broader three-way taxonomy, user-interaction, content-presentation, and data-management applications account for 50%, 25%, and 25% of our benchmark, respectively, compared with approximately 49%, 28%, and 24% of the source collection. The represented classes, with the number of trajectories in each, are Company Brochure Sites (5), Ecommerce Web Applications (4), Analytics Platforms and Dashboards (3), Discussion Forums (3), ERP Platforms (2), Internal Tools (2), Learning Platforms (2), Personal Blog Sites (2), Social Media Platforms (2), Browser-Based Games (1), CRM Systems (1), Email Clients (1), Job Search Platforms (1), News and Information Sites (1), Personal Portfolio Sites (1), and Productivity Applications (1).

Figure 5: Domain coverage of the 32 flows. Application-type distribution of our 32 flows (right) against all 101 WebGen-Bench specifications (left), sharing one colour per class. The legend gives selected over available counts per class. GROUNDING: COLLECTING SIMILAR WEBSITES AND FEATURES Follow-up requests in EVOWEB should reflect how real products actually grow, not how language model imagines they might. We therefore ground each flow in features of existing websites that serve similar purpose to the seed application. Grounding runs once per seed specification, before any request is written, and produces the real-product material that the generator (App. D) later adapts into requests. It is fixed, schema-constrained retrieval procedure executed by language-model agent, Claude Sonnet 4.6, equipped with two tools: web-search tool that returns ranked results for text query, and page-fetch tool that returns the content of URL. The agent receives the seeds one-sentence summary, its full build prompt, and its WebGen-Bench application category, and proceeds in four steps. 1. Query. The agent issues web-search queries for deployed products that serve the same purpose as the seed. Similarity is judged by the agent against the seeds description and category, not by search rank, so the two sites it keeps need not be the first two results. 2. Select. From the results it selects two websites and for each, the product name, its URL, and one-sentence description of what it does. 3. Extract. It fetches each selected site and identifies two to four notable features beyond the seeds core functionality (in practice, 57 of the 64 sites yielded four and 7 yielded three), keeping only features that are implementable in single-page web app, that are progressive enhancements rather than core functionality, that user would plausibly request after seeing the initial app, and that span range of difficulty. 4. Record. For each feature it writes name, description of what the feature does, and concrete follow-up idea phrased as user request. The record is validated against JSON schema that requires exactly two sites per seed and all three fields per feature. Over the 101 WebGen-Bench seeds this yields 202 sites and 801 features, with 195 sites contributing four features and the remaining seven contributing three. The 32 flows of EVOWEB use the records of their seeds. The generator receives these records as its only source of feature ideas and never sees the retrieved pages. The agents instructions are reproduced verbatim below.

sections.title: Value
sections.content: 32 10 5 7.8 4.75 / 6 Feature archetypes. The generator prompt requires every follow-up request to implement one of four archetypes, each with its own hardness condition: derived state, feature that computes, aggregates, or ranks over seeded or earlier records, with the seed arranged so that naive implementation shows visibly different result, interactive tool, feature driven purely by the users typed input whose state updates during the interaction, multi-page workflow, flow that spans two or more views with every action reachable, and design restyle, bundle of four to six visual requirements applied consistently across at least three pages. The prompt asks for at least three archetypes per flow, at most four requests of any one, and no archetype twice in row. Over the 288 follow-up requests of the 32 flows the split is 112 derived state (39%), 77 multi-page workflow (27%), 67 interactive tool (23%), and 32 design restyle (11%), exactly one per flow. Figure 2 colors the requests of one flow by archetype. D.1 GENERATOR SPECIFICATION Inputs. The generator sees the base build prompt and the grounding entry of the app (similar websites and their features, App. C), but never the finished application, so it may not assume any implementation detail beyond what the build prompt requests. It favors grounded features that require real engineering, such as multi-criteria filtering, ranking with ties, aggregations, calculators, or pagination interacting with filters, and admits cosmetic features only within the design-restyle archetype. Feature graph and dependencies. The generator first imagines the app grown into larger product and designs nine major features, each adapted, fused, or extended from grounded feature, and then orders them topologically as requests 210. It records dependency DAG over all ten requests, with request 1 as the base app and an edge for every significant reliance: the later feature could not do what its request asks if the earlier feature were missing or broken. Merely reading the same seeded records does not count as dependency. Edges point only forward and are labeled with what is relied on; the DAG is used for auditing and is never shown to the evaluated agent. Each sequence contains at least three dependencies between follow-up requests and at least one chain of depth at least three from the base app, and every design-restyle request has an edge to each feature it restyles. Dependencies must also be fair: they run only through user-visible behavior that an earlier request explicitly asked for, so any valid implementation of earlier requests supports the later ones. Intrinsic difficulty. Every follow-up must be distinct new capability, different core operation on different UI surface from the base app and from every other request, and must bundle several interacting requirements rather than single control. Its correctness must also hinge on non-trivial sub-problem that shallow implementation gets wrong: boolean composition of criteria, counts that stay consistent with the visible set, stable sorting with ties, exact computed values with correct rounding and units, empty, boundary, or first-load handling, or precise input validation (for design restyles, full cross-page consistency). Depending on an earlier request does not by itself satisfy this requirement.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Pinned seed and global rules. Exactly one early request (request 2 or 3) pins small dataset of about five to eight records with exact names and values, so that later derived-state requests have exact expected results. Three app-wide global rules per flow, such as domain-specific formatting, labeling, or ordering convention, are introduced as user preferences in early requests with an explicitly app-wide scope. Later requests never restate them, so compliance is tested silently. Feasibility and style. Every feature must be implementable as self-contained client-side React application with local seeded data: no external APIs or live data, LLM-based features, messaging, authentication, file upload or download, real-time synchronization, or dependence on the current date, and exports are rendered on screen. Requests are typically written in two to five sentences in casual product-owner voice, refer to earlier work as user would, and embed all exact values conversationally rather than as specification clauses. Verification tests. Each follow-up has exactly five tests in fixed order. Tests 13 are functional and exercise the new request; at least one of them targets its non-trivial sub-problem, and from the pinned-seed request onward, all but two of the benchmarks requests include an exact-value test whose expected constant is computed from the pinned records, with the seed arranged so that naive build shows different constant. Test 4 is an integration test that walks DAG edge into the request, acting on the earlier feature and checking that its effect appears correctly in the new one; for requests with no incoming dependency, this slot instead checks global rule on the new surface. Test 5 is backward test copied verbatim from an earlier request (for request 2, test of the base app), with targets chosen to favor features that later requests rely on; at least five of requests 29 are re-tested later in the sequence. Tests must be executable by the click-and-type browser agent (no hover, drag, sliders, or keyboard navigation) within about six operations, use the simplest interaction that proves the check, and never ask the agent to set up state or invent values; any data test needs is seeded through its request. At most two tests per sequence may check list-count convention. Finally, tests are implementation-agnostic: they reference only elements and values that the requests explicitly asked for, and every expected result must hold for any reasonable implementation of the requests. Construction-time interaction audit. During benchmark construction, to check the tests against the browser evaluator, team of research engineers manually inspected approximately 200 randomly sampled browser-test executions spanning all test types (functional, integration, backward, and global-rule tests), reviewing interaction traces, visual evidence, and assigned scores for consistency with the intended checks. This qualitative audit informed the interaction constraints above: tests exclude hover-dependent behavior, drag-and-drop and drag-to-reorder interactions, keyboard navigation, and controls such as sliders, range handles, and dials; numeric thresholds are instead specified through text inputs, and tests requiring roles or hidden states inaccessible to the evaluator are excluded. These constraints apply to every test type and align the tests with the evaluators supported click-and-type interactions. After these revisions, we conducted the quantitative humanvalidation study described in Appendix D.3. Test satisfiability. To check that the tests can be passed, we pool all runs of the five strongest models (Fable 5, Kimi K3, GPT 5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6). Every verification test receives full score in at least two of these runs. For 284 of the 288 follow-up requests, single application passes all five of the requests tests at the same point in trajectory, showing that the tests are jointly satisfiable. We manually inspected the remaining four requests and found no conflicting requirements: each of their tests is passed individually, though no single run passes all of them at once. Backward-test transitions. Each backward test re-runs test that was already scored when its original request was evaluated. Pooling all runs of all models, we compare each backward tests verdict at that earlier evaluation with its verdict when re-run at later request  (Table 9)  . Of the tests that passed earlier, 94.8% still pass and 5.2% no longer do (3.8% NO, 1.5% PARTIAL), the rate of apparent regressions. Of the tests that failed earlier, 29.0% improve, 21.0% to full pass, reflecting repairs made while implementing later requests. failed backward test therefore does not by itself indicate newly introduced regression. Because both verdicts come from the automated judge, some transitions reflect evaluator variability rather than changes in the application (App. D.3).

D.3 HUMAN VALIDATION OF THE EVALUATOR After the construction-stage revisions to the tests and interaction constraints (App. D.1), we validated the browser evaluator against human judgments. We randomly selected 300 executions from the full evaluation pool, across all models, applications, and request positions, balanced across test types: 100 functional, 100 integration, and 100 backward tests. Integration examples exclude global-rule checks, matching Sec. 5.1. Several research engineers annotated the executions, and each execution received one final human label. Annotators saw the request, the specific test, and the browser agents screenshots and recorded actions; the benchmark verdict was hidden. When the screenshots were insufficient, annotators inspected the application directly; this occurred for 39 executions (13%), and their final labels are included in all results below. sections.title: E EXECUTION DETAILS
sections.content: We run all coding agents in OpenHands with its recommended configuration and budget of at most 20 agent turns per request. The repository and the agents conversation history persist across the ten requests of trajectory. Context compaction is handled by OpenHands. Reasoning and sampling settings for each model follow its vendors recommended settings. For evaluation, each browser test runs in fresh browser session, so no browser state carries over between tests. RUN-TO-RUN VARIABILITY Coding agents are stochastic, so single run may not reflect models typical performance. To measure this variance, we repeat the full evaluation three times for the closed-source models. Table 12 reports the mean and the population standard deviation across three independent runs for the Anthropic and GPT 5.6 models of Table 2, run through the official Anthropic and OpenAI APIs. The open-source models were run once. Fable 5 is the most stable model, with Grade standard deviation of 0.004, while Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.8 vary by about 0.025 between runs, so the 0.001 gap between them in Table 2 is within noise, whereas the gaps between tiers, of 0.05 and more, are about two standard deviations of the noisiest models and wider for the others. With only three runs per model, these standard deviations are themselves coarse estimates. They capture run-to-run variation only, not the choice of the 32 applications, and open-source models were run once, so Grade gaps of about 0.01 (e.g., Fable 5 vs. Kimi K3) do not establish ranking. The language and DAG analyses likewise lack confidence intervals. Table 12: Mean and population standard deviation across three runs for the closed-source models of Table 2.

sections.title: H SENSITIVITY TO USER TOLERANCE
sections.content: We examine how model rankings depend on user tolerance by evaluating the two endpoints of the threshold range defined in Sec. 3.4. At = 0, all requests contribute regardless of earlier outcomes, so delivered functionality reduces to mean request accuracy, Q(0) = R1 (cid:80)R r=1 ar. At = 1, each request contributes only if all preceding requests are fully successful. This yields the fail-stop score Q(1), which retains credit for the first imperfect request and assigns zero to subsequent requests. Grade averages delivered functionality over the full threshold range. Table 13 reports these endpoint scores alongside Grade. Mean accuracy and Grade produce similar rankings, with no model moving more than two positions. The strictest threshold produces larger changes: Qwen3.8 2.4T-A95B ranks ninth by Grade but second by the fail-stop score, while Fable 5 ranks first under all three metrics. These results show that individual model rankings can depend substantially on assuming that users tolerate no imperfect requests. Threshold weighting and early errors. sections.title: I ROBUSTNESS TO THE JUDGE MODEL
sections.content: Every result in this paper is graded by the same LLM-driven browser judge (Sec. 3.3), so we test whether the results depend on which model runs it. LLM judges have been reported to prefer outputs from their own model or model family (Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2024; Wataoka et al., 2024). Judge choice also matters for web agents more broadly: on AgentRewardBench, no single LLM judge is best across benchmarks (L`u et al., 2025). Since our default grader runs on Sonnet 4.6, which is also one of the evaluated agents, we re-evaluate the same runs with three judges from other vendors and compare the resulting Grades  (Table 14)  . Each alternative judge reverses the order of only 2-3 model pairs relative to the default, all among GPT 5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6, which lie within 0.015 Grade of each other under the default judge. We also find no self-preference. Under its own judge, Sonnet 4.6 ranks fifth, below its third place under GPT 5.6 Terra and GLM 5.3 Flash, and GPT 5.6 Terra and GLM 5.2 hold the same rank under their own vendors judges as under every other judge. sections.title: J COMPUTE COST
sections.content: Each model is evaluated on 320 requests (32 flows 10 requests), each with up to 20 agent turns followed by five browser tests, i.e., about 1,600 browser evaluations per model, each multi-step session of screenshot-and-act interactions. Browser verification is CPU-bound: run serially on one

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: machine, single model takes about 20 hours end to end. We execute the 32 flows concurrently, each in dedicated container with six vCPUs. Our Kubernetes-based infrastructure scales to hundreds of vCPUs, providing each sample with an isolated headless browser environment. This distributed architecture enables us to evaluate multiple models in parallel in under two hours. We thank Roei Dalal for his invaluable DevOps contributions to this infrastructure.
